papers.title_in_file: Classical simulation of commuting quantum computations implies collapse of the polynomial hierarchy
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv:1005.1407v1 (9 May 2010), the preprint of Bremner, Jozsa and Shepherd. It is the paper the record names.
sections_read: 2.5 Notions of classical simulation for quantum circuits
3.1 The power of IQP with post-selection
3.2 Classical simulation of IQP circuits and collapse of PH

figures.shows: Two quantum circuit diagrams, no numeric axes. Panel (a): one line carrying the state |alpha>, then a gate U, then an H gate, then a gate V, with output V H U |alpha>. Panel (b): the upper line carries |alpha> through U, then a control dot of a CZ gate, then an H gate, then a post-selection marker <0|; a new lower ancilla line starts in |0>, passes an H gate, then the target of the CZ gate, then a gate V, with output V H U |alpha>. The figure marks the replacement of the intermediate H gate by a CZ gate, a post-selection and two H gates at the ends of lines.
figures.confirmed_by: (somewhat akin to a gate teleportation) illustrated in ﬁgure 1.

papers.what_it_is: A complexity-theory paper that proves post-IQP equals PP and that efficient classical sampling of commuting (IQP) quantum circuits, up to a multiplicative error below the square root of 2, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy to its third level.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that if the output distributions of uniform IQP circuit families could be classically efficiently sampled, even up to 41% multiplicative error in the probabilities, the polynomial hierarchy would collapse to its third level.
quotes: if the output distributions of uniform IQP circuit families could be classically eﬃciently sampled, even up to 41% multiplicative error in the probabilities,
would collapse to its third level.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract summarizes Corollary 1; the statement with its conditions is entered separately from Section 3.2.
assertions.reader_inference: 41% is the abstract's rounding of the bound c < square root of 2 in Theorem 2 and Corollary 1; the body states the bound, not the percentage.

assertions.value: The paper proves Theorem 1: post-IQP equals post-BQP, which equals PP.
quotes: Theorem 1 post-IQP = post-BQP = PP.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states Theorem 1 in Section 3.1 and proves it by a reduction through the Hadamard gadget; the class post-IQP is defined in Definition 3 on p.5.

assertions.value: In the proof that post-IQP equals post-BQP the authors replace each intermediate H gate by an extra qubit line, a CZ gate and a post-selection of outcome 0, and state that an easy calculation shows the resulting state on the extra line is H applied to the input state.
quotes: followed by post-selection of outcome 0 on line a.
An easy calculation shows that the resulting state on line e is H |ψ .
Thus the non-diagonal intermediate H gate has been replaced by a new CZ gate and an additional post-selection.
assertions.certainty_reason: A step of the proof of Theorem 1; the paper asserts the calculation as easy and does not print it.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof step is part of what Theorem 1 rests on; its grade may follow Theorem 1's.

assertions.value: The authors state that SWAP is not a valid IQP gate, so in that construction they commute all SWAP gates to the end of the lines.
quotes: SWAP is not a valid IQP gate so to obtain the ﬁnal circuit we commute out all SWAP gates to the end of the lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: A step of the proof of Theorem 1, stated without a separate derivation.

assertions.value: The proof of Theorem 1 starts from an arbitrary uniform quantum circuit family with gates from a universal set; the authors note all these gates are 1- or 2-qubit gates and, apart from H, have diagonal entries that are integer powers of e to the i pi over 8.
assertions.anchor: Proof of Theorem 1, Section 3.1, p.7; p.8
quotes: uniform quantum circuit family with inputs |0 . . . |0 and with gates drawn from the following
gates are 1- or 2-qubit gates and apart from H, all gates have diagonal entries that are integer powers of eiπ/8.)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the gate set and its properties as the setup of the proof of Theorem 1 (p.7 to p.8).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum part of the IQP process from that construction can be rendered, logically speaking, by local interactions on a flat 2-dimensional surface, while still using the inefficient resource of post-selection.
quotes: can be rendered, logically speaking, by local interactions on a ﬂat 2-dimensional surface (albeit still involving the ineﬃcient resource of post-selection).
assertions.certainty_reason: A remark on the construction, argued in a few lines from Figure 1(b) and not proved formally.

assertions.value: The paper proves Theorem 2: if the output distributions of uniform IQP circuit families could be weakly classically simulated to within multiplicative error c with 1 ≤ c < sqrt(2), then post-BPP = PP.
quotes: Theorem 2 If the output probability distributions generated by uniform fam
of IQP circuits could be weakly classically simulated to within multiplicative error 1 ≤ c < 2 then post-BPP = PP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 is stated with its simulation condition on p.9 and proved on p.9 to p.10 from Theorem 1 and the multiplicative bounds of eq. (8).
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the square root sign apart from its argument, so the bound reads 'c < 2' with the root sign split off; the proof states the condition c squared below 1 plus 2 delta.

assertions.value: In the proof of Theorem 2 the authors conclude that, because the level of error delta can be taken as close to one half as needed, any value of c below the square root of 2 suffices to guarantee that the language L is in post-BPP.
quotes: see that any value of c < 2 will suﬃce to guarantee that L ∈ post-BPP.
Combining this with eq. (5) we see that the classical uniform family
assertions.certainty_reason: A step of the proof of Theorem 2; graded with the theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that a multiplicative approximation suits the quotient structure of the conditional probabilities, whereas an additive or total variation distance approximation would be problematic because the denominators are required only to be positive and could allow catastrophic divergences of the probability quotients.
quotes: In contrast, use of an additive approximation or approximation to within ǫ total variation distance would be problematic

the denominators of eqs. (4) and (7) are required only to be positive, so additive or total variation distance approximations would allow catastrophic divergences of the associated probability quotients.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors explain in words why their method needs multiplicative error; no counterexample is given.

assertions.value: The paper proves Corollary 1: if the output distributions of uniform IQP circuit families could be weakly classically simulated to within multiplicative error c with 1 ≤ c < sqrt(2), then the polynomial hierarchy would collapse to its third level, PH = Delta 3.
quotes: could be weakly classically simulated to within multiplicative error 1 ≤ c < 2 then the polynomial hierarchy would collapse to its third level i.e. PH = ∆3.
Under the simulation assumption we may apply theorem 2, and Toda’s theorem with eq. (3) gives PH ⊆ PPP = Ppost−BPP ⊆ ∆3.
assertions.certainty_reason: Corollary 1 is stated with its condition on p.10 and proved there from Theorem 2, Toda's theorem and eq. (3).
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the square root sign apart from its argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from the proof of Theorem 1, it suffices in Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 to require the weak simulability condition only for IQP circuit families of 1- and 2-qubit gates whose diagonal entries are integer powers of e to the i pi over 8.
quotes: to require the weak simulability condition only for a restricted kind of IQP circuit family, namely those comprising only 1- and 2-qubit gates with diagonal entries being only integer powers of eiπ/8.
assertions.certainty_reason: A consequence the authors draw by inspection of the proof of Theorem 1; no separate proof.

assertions.value: The paper proves Theorem 3: the output distributions of any uniform family of IQP circuits with output registers of size O(log n) can be sampled, without approximation, by a classical randomised process that runs in time O(poly(n)).
quotes: Theorem 3 Let Pw be the output probability distributions for any uniform family of IQP circuits in which the output registers have size O(log n). Then Pw may be sampled (without approximation) by a classical randomised process that runs in time O(poly(n)).
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3 is stated with its condition on p.10 and proved on p.10 to p.11.

assertions.value: In the proof of the log-output theorem the authors state that the phase function can be computed in classical poly(n) time, that a measurement of the complementary register yields a uniformly random bit string, and that the remaining state on the output lines can be strongly simulated by direct calculation, giving an exact weak classical simulation.
assertions.anchor: Proof of Theorem 3, Section 3.2, p.10; p.11
quotes: The phase function f (x, y) can be computed in classical poly(n) time by accumulating the relevant diagonal elements of the successive gates.
a measurement of Yw will yield a uniformly random bit string of length N
giving overall an exact weak classical simulation of the original circuit family
assertions.certainty_reason: Proof steps of Theorem 3; graded with the theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the methods developed in a cited work (reference 11, Van den Nest) may also be used to readily provide a weak classical simulation up to additive polynomial error for the families in the log-output theorem.
quotes: The methods developed in [11] may also be used to readily provide a weak classical simulation up to additive polynomial error for the families in the above theorem.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a cited preprint of Shepherd shows the output distributions in the log-output theorem are even classically strongly simulable if all gates have diagonal entries only integer powers of e to the i pi over 8.
quotes: even more, they are classically strongly simulable, if all the gates are restricted to have diagonal entries of only integer powers of eiπ/8
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to another preprint.

assertions.value: The authors state that BPP with an IQP oracle is contained in BQP, and that Theorem 3 shows BPP with an IQP oracle limited to circuits with at most O(log n) output lines equals BPP.
quotes: it is easy to see that BPPIQP ⊆ BQP, and theorem 3 shows that BPPIQP[log n] = BPP
denotes that the oracle is queried only with IQP circuits having at most O(log n) output lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: A corollary-style remark the authors state without a separate proof; the equality follows from Theorem 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the only feature of IQP needed for the main results was theorem 1, that post-selection boosts its power to PP, so the hardness evidence of Corollary 1 would apply to any class of circuits that goes to PP under post-selection.
quotes: The only feature of IQP that we needed was the result of theorem 1, that post-selection boosts its power to PP.
Thus the evidence of hardness of classical simulation provided by corollary 1 would apply to any class of circuits that similarly goes to PP under post-selection.
assertions.certainty_reason: A generalization the authors state from the structure of their proof, without a formal theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that constructions in cited works (references 13 and 14, using gate teleportation) imply that quantum circuits of depth 4, with 3 layers of unitary gates then a layer of measurements, with post-selection include BQP and hence post-BQP = PP, while circuits of depth 3 are known to be always strongly classically simulable.
quotes: imply that the power of quantum circuits of depth 4 (i.e. 3 layers of unitary gates followed by a layer of measurements) with post-selection includes BQP and hence also post-BQP = PP
while quantum circuits of depth 3 are known to be always strongly classically simulable.
the constructions in [13, 14] (exploiting the notion of gate teleportation [19])
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes these results to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with the class BQNC0 of languages decided with bounded error by uniform families of constant depth circuits, post-BQNC0 = PP, and that the conclusion of Corollary 1 then applies to QNC0 replacing IQP.
quotes: we have post-BQNC0 = PP and the conclusion of our corollary 1 then applies to QNC0 (constant depth quantum circuits) replacing IQP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a consequence of cited constructions, without a separate proof here.

assertions.value: The paper defines a uniform family of circuits as a mapping from a bit string w of length n to a classical description Cw of a circuit of the appropriate type, where the mapping is computable in classical polynomial time in n.
quotes: A uniform family of circuits (of some speciﬁed type) is a mapping w → Cw where w = x1 . . . xn is a bit string of length n, Cw is a (classical) description of a circuit (of the appropriate type) and the mapping w → Cw is computable in classical poly(n) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 1, stated by the paper on p.3.

assertions.value: The paper defines an IQP circuit on n qubit lines as a quantum circuit in which each gate is diagonal in the X basis, the input state is the all-zero state, and the output is the result of a computational basis measurement on a specified set of output lines.
quotes: An IQP circuit on n qubit lines is a quantum circuit with the following structure: each gate in the circuit is diagonal in the X basis
and the output is the result of a computational basis measurement on a speciﬁed set of output lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 2, stated by the paper on p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state they assume each IQP gate is specified by its diagonal entries and the lines it acts on, so that a polynomial-size description implies any gate acts on at most O(log n) lines.
quotes: In this paper we will assume that each gate in the description of an IQP circuit Cw is speciﬁed by giving its diagonal entries and the lines on which it acts.
Thus a poly(n) sized description implies that any gate acts on at most O(log n) lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this convention as the scope of its IQP definition (p.4).

assertions.value: The authors state that an IQP circuit can be represented with gates diagonal in the Z basis, where each qubit line begins and ends with a Hadamard gate and every gate in between is diagonal in the Z basis.
quotes: each qubit line begins and ends with a Hadamard (H) gate, and in between, every gate is diagonal in the Z basis.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this equivalent representation of its Definition 2 and gives the argument in the same paragraph (p.4).

assertions.value: The authors define BPP (resp. PP) as the class of decision tasks decided with bounded error (resp. unbounded error) by uniform families of classical randomised circuits, and BQP as the class solved with bounded error by uniform families of quantum circuits.
quotes: The complexity class of decision tasks decided with bounded error (resp. unbounded error) by uniform families of classical randomised circuits is denoted BPP (resp. PP).
The class of decision tasks solved with bounded error by such uniform families is denoted BQP.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these definitions of the classes on p.4.

assertions.value: The paper defines a language L to be in post-IQP if a uniform family of post-selected IQP circuits, with a single line output register and a post-selection register, gives output 1 with conditional probability at least 1 minus epsilon when w is in L and output 0 with conditional probability at least 1 minus epsilon when w is not in L, given the post-selection register reads all zeros, for some error tolerance epsilon below one half.
quotes: A language L is in the class post-IQP (resp. post-BQP or post-BPP) iﬀ there
(i) if w ∈ L then prob [Ow = 1|Pw = 00 . . . 0] ≥ 1 − ǫ and
(ii) if w ∈/ L then prob [Ow = 0|Pw = 00 . . . 0] ≥ 1 − ǫ.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 3, stated by the paper on p.5.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound epsilon below one half is printed on separate lines of the text layer, so it is not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since no limit is placed on how small the non-zero post-selection probability may be, post-selection may incur an exponential overhead in time and is principally of interest as a theoretical tool rather than a feasible computational resource.
quotes: the post-selection process may incur an exponential overhead in time, and similar to the notion of a non-deterministic computation, it is principally of interest as a theoretical tool rather than as a feasible computational resource.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of post-selection as a computational resource on p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the class post-IQP is independent of the error tolerance epsilon, as will follow from Theorem 1, but that the class BIQP with error epsilon, without post-selection, is not known to be independent of epsilon.
quotes: of ǫ, as will follow from theorem 1 below.
However the class BIQPǫ of languages decided with bounded error ǫ by uniform families of IQP circuits (with no post-selection) is not known to be
assertions.certainty_reason: The independence of post-IQP is derived from Theorem 1; the second half states an open point.
assertions.reader_inference: This value joins two claims, a derived result and an open point; the review may split it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the class BPPpath, studied extensively in a cited work (reference 16), is easily seen to equal their class post-BPP.
quotes: The class called BPPpath that is extensively studied in [16] is easily seen to be equal to our class post-BPP.
assertions.certainty_reason: A relation to a cited work, stated as easily seen without proof.

assertions.value: The paper defines a circuit family as strongly simulable if any output probability and any marginal probability of Pw can be computed to m digits of precision in classical poly(n, m) time.
quotes: We say that a circuit family is strongly simulable if any output probability in Pw and any marginal probability of Pw can be computed to m digits of precision in classical poly(n, m) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition (a) of Section 2.5, p.6.

assertions.value: The paper defines a circuit family as weakly simulable if, given the description of Cw, its output distribution Pw can be sampled by purely classical means in poly(n) time.
quotes: A circuit family is weakly simulable if given the description of Cw, its output distribution Pw can be sampled by purely classical means in poly(n) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition (b) of Section 2.5, p.6.

assertions.value: The authors note, citing earlier work, that strong simulability implies weak simulability, because the output can be sampled bit by bit from conditional distributions computed as quotients of two marginal probabilities.
quotes: Note that strong simulability implies weak simulability [13]
the binary distribution used for each successive bit is the conditional distribution, conditioned on the already seen values
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the implication to other work and sketches the argument.

assertions.value: The paper defines a circuit family as weakly simulable with multiplicative error c ≥ 1 if there is a family Rw of distributions on the same sample spaces as Pw that can be sampled in classical polynomial time and, for all x and w, whose probabilities lie within a factor c of those of Pw in both directions.
quotes: A circuit family is weakly simulable with multiplicative error c ≥ 1 if there is a family Rw of distributions (on the same sample spaces as Pw) such that Rw can be sampled in classical poly(n) time and for all x and w we have
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition (c) of Section 2.5, p.6; the bounds are the paper's eq. (2), which the text layer prints in fragments.
assertions.reader_inference: The factor-c bounds are read from eq. (2) in the text layer fragments, not quoted.

assertions.value: The paper defines a circuit family as weakly simulable within epsilon total variation distance if there is a family Rw as in the multiplicative-error definition but with the multiplicative condition replaced by a bound on the total variation distance.
quotes: A circuit family is weakly simulable within ǫ total variation distance if there is a family Rw as in (c) above
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition (d) of Section 2.5, p.6.

assertions.value: The paper defines a circuit family as classically weakly simulatable with additive polynomial error if the estimates of output probabilities that a quantum process gives to within one over any polynomial can be obtained from the circuit descriptions by purely classical means in poly(n) time.
quotes: We say that a circuit family is (classically) weakly simulatable with additive polynomial error if the same estimates can be obtained from the circuit descriptions Cw by purely classical means in poly(n) time
for any polynomial f (n) we can output p˜ such that |p − p˜| < 1/f (n).
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition (e) of Section 2.5, p.6; the notion is attributed to a cited work (reference 11).

assertions.value: The authors state that the existence of a weak simulation with additive polynomial error, or with multiplicative error 1 ≤ c < 2(1 minus epsilon), of a circuit family that decides a language L with bounded error will also imply that L is in BPP.
quotes: Similarly the existence of a weak simulation with additive polynomial error, or with
multiplicative error 1 ≤ c < 2(1 − ǫ), will also imply that L ∈ BPP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an immediate consequence with the reason that the simulated family still decides L with bounded error; not set out as a numbered result.

assertions.value: The authors define the polynomial hierarchy class PH as the union of an infinite tower of increasing classes Delta k, k = 1, 2, ..., in which Delta 1 = P and Delta k plus 1 is P with an oracle for the nondeterministic class associated to Delta k.
quotes: The polynomial hierarchy class PH [7, 8] is deﬁned to be the union of an inﬁnite tower of increasing classes ∆k, k = 1, 2, . . ., in which ∆1 = P and ∆k+1 = PN∆k.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this definition on p.7, citing standard texts.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that BPP is contained in N Delta 2 and that post-BPP is contained in Delta 3.
quotes: For classical computation it is known [7, 8] that BPP is contained in N∆2 and also that post-BPP is contained in ∆3 [16].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes these inclusions to cited works.

assertions.value: The authors derive eq. (3): P with an oracle for post-BPP is contained in P with an oracle for Delta 3, which equals Delta 3.
quotes: Ppost−BPP ⊆ P∆3 = ∆3.
Now for any complexity class C we have P(PC) = PC
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in two lines from cited inclusions; not a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Toda's theorem, that PH is contained in P with an oracle for PP, so P with an oracle for post-BQP contains PH.
quotes: A theorem of Toda [9, 7, 8] asserts that PH⊆PPP so we get Ppost−BQP ⊇ PH.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited theorem; a consequence is drawn by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that Aaronson has shown that adding post-selection to universal polynomial time quantum computation boosts the computational power from BQP to the classical class PP.
quotes: Aaronson [6] has shown that if post-selection is included with universal polynomial time quantum computation then the computational power is boosted from BQP to the classical class PP.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to Aaronson's earlier work.

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier work (references 13 and 14) showed that the existence of strong simulations for some classes of quantum computations would imply the collapse of the polynomial hierarchy.
quotes: Previously it was known [13, 14] that the existence of such strong simulations for some classes of quantum computations would imply the collapse of the polynomial hierarchy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to cited works.

assertions.value: The authors state that the notion of classical simulation in their main result is an especially weak one, and that their result contrasts with earlier strong-simulation results in the simplicity of the quantum processes and the much weaker requirements on the classical simulation.
quotes: The notion of classical simulation that applies in our main result is an especially weak one
Our result contrasts with these works in the striking simplicity of the quantum processes being considered and in the very much weaker requirements in the classical simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's characterization of their own result in the introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that circuits of only commuting gates are of significance for super- and semi-conductor qubit implementations, where a cited work (reference 5) has recently shown they are much simpler to implement fault-tolerantly than gates from a fully universal set.
quotes: where it has recently been shown [5] that they are much simpler to implement fault-tolerantly than gates drawn from a fully universal set.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the result to a cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy would not imply P=NP, but is nevertheless widely regarded as similarly implausible.
quotes: While not implying that P=NP, such a collapse is nevertheless widely regarded as being similarly implausible.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement about the standing of the hardness evidence, without argument in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion of the paper is conditional evidence of hardness, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because proof of classical hardness is notoriously difficult, it has become popular to prove only that if a problem were classically easy it would entail consequences that are highly implausible although generally unproven.
quotes: we prove that if a certain problem were classically easy then this would entail consequences that are highly implausible (although also generally unproven)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the kind of evidence it provides, which limits what its results show (p.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that there is as yet no theoretical proof that any quantum algorithm outperforms the best classical algorithm for the task in the standard setting of polynomial against exponential running time, without oracles or communication.
quotes: there is yet no theoretical proof that any quantum algorithm outperforms the best classical algorithm for the task, in the standard computational setting of polynomial vs. exponential running time
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the state of the field in the introduction (2010).
